blocks.text: Long networks can require substantial memory to retain tensors for backward. A checkpoint marks a region whose internal tensors can be recomputed from its inputs. The lower-memory strategy repeats some forward computation during backward. This creates a trade-off between retained activation memory and extra arithmetic, while preserving the derivative.
Evaluate a differentiable block with non-reentrant activation checkpointing, preserving random state for recomputation.

An activation is an intermediate tensor in a forward computation. Backward uses selected forward information to evaluate derivatives. Checkpointing changes which intermediate tensors are retained and which are reconstructed later; it does not change the mathematical objective.

The diagram shows a deliberately simplified chain of six conceptual blocks. Its saved-output and evaluation-count bars describe a chosen schedule, not measured PyTorch bytes or a universal checkpoint schedule. Actual non-reentrant checkpointing can stop recomputation when the required tensors have been recovered. Kernel fusion, shared tensors, and tensor sizes also affect real memory use.

blocks.caption: f is the differentiable block and L is the downstream objective. Equality assumes that recomputation is consistent with the original forward pass.

blocks.text: The supplied wrapper explicitly selects non-reentrant checkpointing and preserves random state. Randomness matters when a block contains operations such as dropout. If recomputation sampled an unrelated mask, the backward pass could describe a different computation. Preserving RNG state helps reproduce the original randomized operations under the checkpoint implementation’s supported device behavior.

The final step checks real gradients for sin(x) times sigmoid(x) with and without the supplied checkpoint wrapper. Equal gradients establish the intended invariant for that example. They do not establish a memory saving for every block. Avoid stateful side effects inside a recomputed block, because it may run more than once. Test memory and runtime separately on the actual model before claiming a practical speed or capacity improvement.
